cards.q: What is the difference between retained and immediate mode?
cards.a:
Retained mode keeps widget objects you update; immediate mode describes the UI each frame

In immediate mode there are no widget objects for you to keep: each frame's calls read and write your data directly and return what the user did.

cards.q: Does Dear ImGui keep any state between frames?
cards.a:
Yes: interface state such as window positions and open tree nodes, found by ID

"Immediate mode" describes the API, not the insides. ImGui keeps interface state (window positions and sizes, open nodes, the active widget, scroll and text editing) looked up by ID, but never a copy of your data.

cards.q: Why does immediate mode avoid synchronisation bugs?
cards.a:
Because widgets read and write the program's real data directly every frame, so there is no second copy

With `SliderFloat("Speed", &player.speed, ...)` the slider shows and changes `player.speed` itself; there is no widget value to keep in step.

cards.q: What does ImGui::Button return?
cards.a:
true on the frame the button was clicked

Immediate-mode functions return what the user did this frame; there is no button object to keep.

cards.q: A value changes in the game. What must you do so an ImGui slider shows the new value?
cards.a:
Nothing; the slider is drawn from the value again next frame

The slider reads the real variable every frame, so there is no copy to keep in sync.

cards.q: Which of these is a poor fit for Dear ImGui?
cards.a:
A heavily styled main menu shown to players with a controller

Tools are its strength; polished, animated, player-facing UI is usually better served by a retained toolkit or a hand-made UI.

cards.q: Which files make up a typical Win32 + DirectX 11 ImGui set-up?
cards.a:
The ImGui core .cpp and .h files plus imgui_impl_win32 and imgui_impl_dx11 from the backends folder

You compile the core files into your program and add one platform back end (Win32) and one renderer back end (DX11) from backends/.
cards.lessonTitle: Setting Up ImGui with Win32 and DirectX 11

cards.q: List the calls at the start and end of every frame.
cards.a:
Both back ends' NewFrame, then ImGui::NewFrame; ImGui::Render, then the DX11 RenderDrawData

Start with ImGui_ImplDX11_NewFrame, ImGui_ImplWin32_NewFrame and ImGui::NewFrame; end with ImGui::Render and ImGui_ImplDX11_RenderDrawData(ImGui::GetDrawData()). Render only builds the draw data; the renderer back end draws it.
cards.lessonTitle: Setting Up ImGui with Win32 and DirectX 11

cards.q: In what order do you shut ImGui down?
cards.a:
The renderer back end, the platform back end, then DestroyContext: the reverse of setting up

Shut down in the reverse order of setting up, so nothing uses the context after it is gone.
cards.lessonTitle: Setting Up ImGui with Win32 and DirectX 11

cards.q: What does the renderer back end do?
cards.a:
Draws ImGui's triangles and textures with your graphics API

The platform back end handles input and the window; the renderer back end draws.
cards.lessonTitle: Setting Up ImGui with Win32 and DirectX 11

cards.q: Where must ImGui_ImplWin32_WndProcHandler be called?
cards.a:
At the start of your window procedure, so ImGui sees input first

It turns every window message into ImGui input, so it must see each message as it arrives.
cards.lessonTitle: Setting Up ImGui with Win32 and DirectX 11

cards.q: When should a game draw ImGui?
cards.a:
After its own scene, so the interface appears on top

ImGui's draw data is rendered over the finished frame, just before Present.
cards.lessonTitle: Setting Up ImGui with Win32 and DirectX 11

cards.q: What is ImDrawData?
cards.a:
Per-window lists of vertices, indices and draw commands for this frame

It is everything ImGui wants drawn: each draw command also names its texture and clipping rectangle. ImGui::Render collects every window's draw list into one ImDrawData, and the renderer back end turns it into GPU draw calls.
cards.lessonTitle: The Frame and the Draw Data

cards.q: What is a font atlas?
cards.a:
One texture holding every glyph of the loaded fonts, so text can be drawn as textured triangles

It is built at start-up; text then needs nothing special from the back end.
cards.lessonTitle: The Frame and the Draw Data

cards.q: What is io.DeltaTime used for?
cards.a:
The time since the last frame, used for double clicks, key repeat, cursor blinking and animations

The platform back end measures it each frame. The averaged frame rate is a different field, `io.Framerate`.
cards.lessonTitle: The Frame and the Draw Data

cards.q: What does a widget function do in one call?
cards.a:
Lays itself out, handles input, adds shapes, and returns the result

Layout, input and adding shapes to the draw list happen together, immediately; the actual drawing happens later from the draw data.
cards.lessonTitle: The Frame and the Draw Data

cards.q: Why can ImGui run on almost any graphics API?
cards.a:
It only needs textured, coloured triangles with scissor rectangles drawn

A back end is a small piece of code that draws ImDrawData with one API.
cards.lessonTitle: The Frame and the Draw Data

cards.q: How should a standalone tool avoid using a full CPU core while idle?
cards.a:
Wait for input when nothing changes, and use v-sync

A tool only needs to redraw when something happens; skipping parts of a frame breaks ImGui's frame rules.
cards.lessonTitle: The Frame and the Draw Data

cards.q: What does Begin's return value mean, and what must you always do afterwards?
cards.a:
Whether the window's contents are visible (not collapsed or clipped); End must always be called

For windows, End is always paired with Begin. Calling End only when Begin returned true is the rule for most other Begin functions, not for windows.

cards.q: How do you give a window a default size the user can change?
cards.a:
SetNextWindowSize with ImGuiCond_FirstUseEver before Begin

FirstUseEver applies only if the window has never existed. Always would reset the size every frame, so the user could not change it.

cards.q: When does ImGui::Button return true?
cards.a:
On the frame the mouse button is released over it after being pressed over it

Pressing, dragging away and releasing elsewhere does not click it.

cards.q: Begin returns false because the window is collapsed. What must you still do?
cards.a:
Call End

For windows, End is always paired with Begin, whatever Begin returned.

cards.q: What does ImGuiCond_FirstUseEver mean for SetNextWindowSize?
cards.a:
Use it only if the window has no saved settings yet

It applies only if the window has never existed, not even in imgui.ini, so it sets a default without overriding what the user chose. Once per run is ImGuiCond_Once.

cards.q: Why is ImGui::Text(name) with a player's name dangerous?
cards.a:
The name is used as a printf format string, so a % in it reads garbage

Use TextUnformatted(name) or Text("%s", name).

cards.q: How does ImGui compute a widget's ID?
cards.a:
It hashes the widget's label (or the part from ### on), seeded with the value on top of the ID stack, which windows and PushID change

Because the ID comes from the label and the stack, the same label in the same place gives the same ID every frame.

cards.q: What do ## and ### do in a label?
cards.a:
## hides the rest from view but keeps it in the ID; ### uses only the rest as the ID

"Delete##3" shows "Delete" and hashes the whole string; "HP: 87###hp" shows "HP: 87" and hashes only "###hp".

cards.q: What goes wrong if a widget's ID changes every frame?
cards.a:
It loses its remembered state, so drags stop and tree nodes close

State such as open, active or the text cursor is found by ID; a new ID means starting from nothing every frame, so text editing resets too. Use ### with a fixed part.

cards.q: Two buttons labelled "Delete" are drawn in the same window without PushID. What happens?
cards.a:
They share one ID, so clicking one can trigger the other or only the first works

IDs come from labels, not positions; the same label gives the same ID.

cards.q: What is shown and what is hashed for the label "Gold: 50###gold"?
cards.a:
Shown "Gold: 50"; hashed "###gold"

### keeps the ID stable while the visible text changes.

cards.q: Why does PushID(&stone) work well in a loop?
cards.a:
The address is unique for each stone and stays the same between frames

A good ID source is unique and stable. (If stones move in memory, for example when a vector grows, the IDs change too.)

cards.q: Which list names debugging tools built into ImGui?
cards.a:
ShowDemoWindow, the style editor, the Metrics/Debugger window (with its debug log and Item Picker), and the ID Stack tool

All four ship with ImGui itself and open from the demo window's Tools menu. Profilers and graphics debuggers are separate programs.
cards.lessonTitle: The Demo Window and the Debug Tools

cards.q: What should you do when an IM_ASSERT fires?
cards.a:
Read the comment above it in the source, which explains the rule, and fix the code that broke it

The assert reports a real mistake (an unmatched Begin/End or PushID/PopID, a call outside a frame). Silencing it only moves the crash elsewhere.
cards.lessonTitle: The Demo Window and the Debug Tools

cards.q: Why keep imgui_demo.cpp in the project during development?
cards.a:
It shows every feature, and costs nothing unless ShowDemoWindow is called

Find a feature in the demo window, then search imgui_demo.cpp for its label to see the code. Leave the call out of shipping builds.
cards.lessonTitle: The Demo Window and the Debug Tools

cards.q: What is the quickest way to find example code for a widget you saw in ShowDemoWindow?
cards.a:
Search imgui_demo.cpp for the label shown in the demo

The demo is the documentation, with its source beside it.
cards.lessonTitle: The Demo Window and the Debug Tools

cards.q: Which tool tells you why two widgets share an ID?
cards.a:
The ID Stack tool

It shows each level of the ID stack for the hovered widget: the window's seed, every PushID and the label.
cards.lessonTitle: The Demo Window and the Debug Tools

cards.q: You cannot find which function draws a misbehaving widget. What helps?
cards.a:
The Item Picker, which breaks into the code that drew the widget you click

It is in the Metrics window's Tools and breaks into the debugger at the drawing code. The I/O debug log shows input events, not where a widget is drawn.
cards.lessonTitle: The Demo Window and the Debug Tools

cards.q: How does a linear slider map the mouse position to a value?
cards.a:
t = (mouse x minus track start) / track width, clamped to 0..1; value = min + t * (max - min)

The position becomes a fraction of the track, and the fraction picks a point between min and max. Placing the grab goes back with t = (value - min) / (max - min).

cards.q: What does ImGuiSliderFlags_Logarithmic change?
cards.a:
The position maps to the logarithm of the value, giving equal room to each order of magnitude

With it, 0.01 to 0.1 gets as much width as 100 to 1000. The format string is unchanged.

cards.q: Which IsItem function and meaning go together?
cards.a:
IsItemDeactivatedAfterEdit: the edit just finished and it changed the value

IsItemHovered means the mouse is over it, IsItemActive that it is being used now, IsItemActivated that use started this frame, and IsItemDeactivatedAfterEdit that the edit just ended with a change.

cards.q: A slider from 0 to 20 is 200 pixels wide. The mouse is 50 pixels from its start. What value does it set?
When should you use a drag instead of a slider?
cards.a:
For values with no natural limits, or where space is short

Drags change by a speed per pixel and need no track. A slider suits a value with a fixed min and max.

cards.q: How do you record one undo step for a whole drag?
cards.a:
Check ImGui::IsItemDeactivatedAfterEdit() after the widget

It is true once, when the edit ends and the value changed. The return value is true on every frame of the drag, which would record many steps.

cards.q: How do you edit a std::string with InputText?
cards.a:
Include misc/cpp/imgui_stdlib and pass a pointer to the string; it resizes as you type

The imgui_stdlib overloads take a `std::string*` and resize it. `c_str()` is read-only, and the core InputText never resizes a buffer.

cards.q: Which of these flags change what InputText accepts or how it behaves?
cards.a:
CharsDecimal, CharsUppercase, EnterReturnsTrue and Password

AlwaysClamp and Logarithmic are slider flags, and NoResize and NoMove are window flags. Other text flags include CharsHexadecimal, CharsNoBlank and ReadOnly.

cards.q: What is the pattern for validated editing?
cards.a:
Edit a copy, show the validation message as you type, and copy it back only when the edit finishes and the value is valid

Half-typed values never reach your data. A character filter sees one character at a time, not the whole value.

cards.q: Which flag makes InputText return true only when Enter is pressed?
cards.a:
ImGuiInputTextFlags_EnterReturnsTrue

Ideal for console commands and search boxes. CallbackCompletion is called when Tab is pressed.

cards.q: What does a CallbackCharFilter return to reject a character?
cards.a:
1

Returning nonzero discards the typed character; returning 0 keeps it.

cards.q: What is the difference between filtering and validating?
cards.a:
Filtering stops individual characters as they are typed; validating checks the whole value

A name can contain only allowed characters and still be invalid as a whole, for example when it is empty or already taken.

cards.q: What does Selectable do and where is it used?
cards.a:
Draws a full-width clickable row that can show as selected; used in many list widgets

Selectable is the building block of combos, list boxes, tables and trees; you decide which row counts as selected.

cards.q: When would you use BeginCombo instead of the one-line Combo?
cards.a:
When items are not a simple string array, such as a vector of objects

The one-line Combo takes an array of strings or a "\0"-separated string; BeginCombo lets you draw anything inside, such as objects, items with extra drawing or a filtered list.

cards.q: What makes a good filter for a long list?
cards.a:
Case-insensitive matching where every word of the filter appears somewhere in the item, in any order

Then "rock big" finds "big_mossy_rock", which a prefix or exact-substring match would miss.

cards.q: When is EndCombo called?
cards.a:
Only when BeginCombo returned true

BeginCombo returns true while the drop-down is open; calling EndCombo otherwise makes ImGui assert.

cards.q: Why add a static_assert next to an enum's name table?
cards.a:
So the build fails if an enum value is added without a matching name

The table and the enum must stay the same length, and the check costs nothing at run time.

cards.q: How do you size a list box to show eight items?
cards.a:
Use 8 * ImGui::GetTextLineHeightWithSpacing() as its height

The size is in pixels, and measuring in lines adapts to the font size.

cards.q: What are ImGui's two forms of colour, and where is each used?
cards.a:
ImVec4, four floats 0..1, used by widgets and styles; ImU32, four packed bytes, used by draw lists

Widgets and styles edit ImVec4 floats; draw lists store a compact ImU32 per vertex. Both carry alpha.

cards.q: Why does IM_COL32 put red in the lowest byte?
cards.a:
So that in memory on a little-endian machine the bytes are R, G, B, A, the vertex colour format the GPU reads

The lowest byte comes first in memory on a little-endian PC. That is why the hexadecimal number looks backwards: opaque red is 0xFF0000FF.

cards.q: How do you give each of many items a distinct colour?
cards.a:
Spread hues by the golden ratio (i * 0.618 mod 1) at fixed saturation and value

Golden-ratio hues spread evenly however many items there are; convert each HSV colour to RGB. Random colours change every frame and can land close together.

cards.q: What does IM_COL32(255, 0, 0, 255) equal with ImGui's default byte order?
cards.a:
0xFF0000FF

Alpha in the top byte, then blue, green, and red in the lowest byte.

cards.q: Why do draw lists use ImU32 instead of ImVec4?
cards.a:
Four bytes per vertex colour is far smaller than four floats

Every vertex carries a colour, so the saving adds up over millions of vertices.

cards.q: Which colour space makes "rotate through the rainbow at the same brightness" easy?
cards.a:
HSV

In HSV you change only the hue and keep saturation and value.

cards.q: What is the rule for sharing input between ImGui and a game?
cards.a:
Give ImGui the input first; the game uses only what ImGui does not want

The game handles the mouse only when WantCaptureMouse is false and the keyboard only when WantCaptureKeyboard is false. Otherwise typing in a text field also walks the player around.

cards.q: Which of these are input queries ImGui offers your code?
cards.a:
IsKeyPressed, IsKeyDown, IsMouseClicked, IsMouseDragging and GetMousePos

They read the same input the back end fed ImGui. GetAsyncKeyState and GetCursorPos are Win32 functions, and the IsItem functions ask about the last widget, not the keys.

cards.q: Why prefer ImGui::Shortcut over checking keys yourself in a tool?
cards.a:
It respects focus, so shortcuts do not fire while you type elsewhere

It also routes keys and handles modifiers consistently. IsKeyDown reads held keys too, but ignores focus; menu items show shortcut text, yet do not trigger it.

cards.q: The player is typing a level name in an ImGui text field. Which flag tells the game to ignore the keyboard?
cards.a:
io.WantCaptureKeyboard

It is true while an ImGui widget has keyboard focus. WantTextInput is for showing an on-screen keyboard.

cards.q: The mouse is over an ImGui window and the player clicks. Should the game fire?
cards.a:
No; io.WantCaptureMouse is true

ImGui gets first claim on the input.

cards.q: Which call checks the shortcut Ctrl+S with ImGui's focus rules?
cards.a:
ImGui::Shortcut(ImGuiMod_Ctrl | ImGuiKey_S)

MenuItem only shows the text, and IsKeyDown ignores Ctrl and focus; Shortcut detects the keys.

cards.q: How does ImGui decide where a widget goes?
cards.a:
At the window's layout cursor, which moves to the next line after each widget unless SameLine or other layout calls change it

Widgets stack vertically because the cursor moves down after each one. Layout happens immediately, widget by widget.

cards.q: Why measure sizes from the font and the available region?
cards.a:
So the layout adapts to other font sizes, display scaling and window sizes

A fixed 120 pixels looks cramped once someone raises the font size; GetFontSize() * 10 grows with it.

cards.q: What does a group do?
cards.a:
It makes several widgets act as one item for layout and item queries

After EndGroup, SameLine puts the next widget to the right of the whole group, and IsItemHovered asks about all of it.

cards.q: Which call puts the next widget to the right of the previous one?
cards.a:
ImGui::SameLine()

SameLine moves the cursor back up to the end of the last item. Indent moves the left edge of following lines.

cards.q: What does a width of -FLT_MIN mean for PushItemWidth?
cards.a:
Fill up to the right edge of the window

It is ImGui's idiom for "all the space that is left". Hide the label with ## or it is pushed off the edge.

cards.q: Why use BeginDisabled instead of hiding a button?
cards.a:
The user sees the action exists and that it cannot be used right now

Make it clear why with a tooltip.

cards.q: What does a negative child size mean?
cards.a:
Fill the available space minus that amount, leaving room for widgets after the child

0 fills all the space, a positive number is a fixed size, and a negative one fills minus that much.

cards.q: How does ImGuiListClipper make a huge list cheap?
cards.a:
It computes which equal-height items are visible from the scroll position and draws only those, while reserving space for the rest

Only the visible items are drawn, so the cost depends on the window height, not the list length, and the scroll bar still behaves as if all items were there.

cards.q: How do you make a log follow new lines without fighting the user?
cards.a:
Scroll to the bottom only if it was already at the bottom

Check whether the scroll is at the bottom before adding lines. Scrolling down every frame drags the user away from whatever they scrolled up to read.

cards.q: A child should fill the window except for 40 pixels of buttons below it. What height do you pass?
cards.a:
-40

Negative sizes mean "fill, minus this much"; 0 would fill everything and push the buttons out of view.

cards.q: What must be true of the items for ImGuiListClipper to work?
cards.a:
They all have the same height

It computes the visible range from a fixed item height. For variable heights you need a prefix sum of heights instead.

cards.q: With items 20 pixels high, scrolled to y = 1000, what is the first visible item?
cards.a:
50

floor(1000 / 20) = 50, counting items from 0.

cards.q: What does TableSetupScrollFreeze(0, 1) do?
cards.a:
Keeps the first row, normally the headers, visible while the table scrolls

The arguments are columns then rows to freeze: 0 columns and 1 row.

cards.q: How do you sort a table's data?
cards.a:
When TableGetSortSpecs reports SpecsDirty, sort by its specs, then clear the flag

After setting up the columns, compare column by column in spec order, each in its direction. ImGui only reports what the user asked for, and sorting every frame wastes time.

cards.q: Why compare by a column's user ID rather than its index?
cards.a:
A user ID names the column's meaning, so the comparison stays right even if the columns your code sets up change

ColumnIndex is the column's place in your TableSetupColumn calls; if optional columns come and go, the indexes shift but a user ID does not.

cards.q: When BeginTable returns false, what do you do?
cards.a:
Skip the table and do not call EndTable

Tables follow the "End only if Begin returned true" rule.

cards.q: With SortMulti, the user sorts by Team, then Shift-clicks HP. What is Specs[1]?
cards.a:
HP, which breaks ties between rows with the same Team

Specs are in order of priority: Specs[0] is the primary key.

cards.q: Who sorts the rows of an ImGui table?
cards.a:
Your code, using the sort specs when they are dirty

ImGui reports the requested order; you apply it to your data.

cards.q: What are the Leaf and NoTreePushOnOpen flags for?
cards.a:
Leaf draws a node without an arrow for items with no children; NoTreePushOnOpen means TreePop must not be called for it

With NoTreePushOnOpen the node does not push onto the tree stack when open, so there is nothing to pop.

cards.q: What is the anchor in multi-selection?
cards.a:
The last item clicked without Shift; Shift+click selects from it to the clicked item in display order

A plain click or a Ctrl+click moves the anchor; a Shift+click does not.

cards.q: How do you open a tree node from code to reveal a selected object?
cards.a:
Call SetNextItemOpen(true) before drawing each of its ancestors

Every ancestor must be open for the object to appear. DefaultOpen only applies the first time a node is seen.

cards.q: What does ImGuiTreeNodeFlags_OpenOnArrow change?
cards.a:
Only clicking the arrow opens the node, so clicking the label can select it

It separates opening from selecting; check IsItemToggledOpen so the arrow click does not also select.

cards.q: The anchor is item 3 and the user Shift+clicks item 7. What is selected?
cards.a:
Items 3 to 7, replacing the previous selection

Shift+click selects the range from the anchor in display order; Ctrl+Shift+click would add it to the existing selection instead.

cards.q: Why store selected items by ID rather than by row number?
cards.a:
Rows change with sorting, filtering and opening nodes; IDs do not

The selection must survive changes to what is shown.

cards.q: Which pairs follow the "End only if Begin returned true" rule in this lesson?
cards.a:
BeginTabBar/EndTabBar, BeginTabItem/EndTabItem, and BeginItemTooltip/EndTooltip

BeginTabItem returns true only for the visible tab, so EndTabItem goes inside the if. Only windows and child windows always need their End.

cards.q: How do you select a tab from code?
cards.a:
Pass ImGuiTabItemFlags_SetSelected to its BeginTabItem on that frame

The flag applies on the frame you pass it; the order you submit tabs in does not choose the selected one.

cards.q: Why wrap tooltip text?
cards.a:
Long unwrapped text makes the tooltip wider than the screen

Pushing a wrap position keeps it readable: PushTextWrapPos(GetFontSize() * 30) wraps at about 30 characters wide.

cards.q: What is the difference between CollapsingHeader and TreeNode?
cards.a:
CollapsingHeader does not push the ID stack and needs no TreePop

It is a full-width, header-style section toggle; TreeNode pushes the ID stack while open and needs TreePop.

cards.q: Which call shows a simple tooltip for the widget just drawn?
cards.a:
ImGui::SetItemTooltip("...")

It shows only when the last item is hovered. An unchecked BeginTooltip would show all the time.

cards.q: You find ImGui::Columns(2) in old code. What should you consider?
cards.a:
Converting it to a two-column table

Columns is legacy and still works; tables do everything it did and more.

cards.q: Which menu functions follow the "End only if Begin returned true" rule?
cards.a:
BeginMainMenuBar/EndMainMenuBar, BeginMenuBar/EndMenuBar and BeginMenu/EndMenu

All three menu pairs are ended only when their Begin returned true. `Begin`/`End` for windows is the exception that always calls `End`.

cards.q: How do you make a menu's shortcut actually work?
cards.a:
Check the key chord yourself, for example with `ImGui::Shortcut`, once per frame outside the menu code

The shortcut text is only a label. Checking the keys inside the menu block would only work while the menu is open.

cards.q: Why build menus from a command table?
cards.a:
One list drives the menu, shortcuts and palette, and catches shortcut clashes

The table is your own design, not something ImGui needs; its value is that everything about a command, including when it is available, lives in one place.

cards.q: BeginMenu("File") returns false because the menu is closed. What do you do?
cards.a:
Skip its items and do not call EndMenu

Menus follow the "End only if Begin returned true" rule; calling EndMenu after a false Begin makes ImGui assert.

cards.q: What does the "Ctrl+S" argument of MenuItem do?
cards.a:
It is shown next to the item; it does not detect the keys

It is display text only. Detect the shortcut separately.

cards.q: Which MenuItem form toggles a bool when clicked?
cards.a:
`MenuItem(label, shortcut, &flag)`

The `bool*` form flips the bool for you, which is ideal for showing and hiding windows. The `bool` forms only draw a checkmark or enable the item.

cards.q: Describe ImGui's popup model.
cards.a:
A popup has an ID; OpenPopup marks it open once, and BeginPopup, called every frame, returns true and draws it while it is open

Opening is an event, drawing happens every frame. The popup closes on outside clicks, Escape, a Selectable or MenuItem inside it, or CloseCurrentPopup.

cards.q: What do BeginPopupContextItem and BeginPopupContextWindow do?
cards.a:
They open and begin a popup when the item just drawn, or empty space in the window, is right-clicked

They do the OpenPopup call for you on a right-click, then work like BeginPopup, so EndPopup still goes inside the if.

cards.q: How do you centre a modal each time it appears?
cards.a:
SetNextWindowPos at the main viewport's centre, with pivot (0.5, 0.5) and ImGuiCond_Appearing

The pivot puts the window's middle, not its corner, on the point, and ImGuiCond_Appearing applies it each time it opens while still letting the user move it.

cards.q: How often do you call OpenPopup and BeginPopup?
cards.a:
OpenPopup once when it should open; BeginPopup every frame

Calling OpenPopup every frame keeps reopening and resetting the popup; BeginPopup must run every frame to draw it.

cards.q: OpenPopup("menu") is called inside PushID(3), BeginPopup("menu") outside it. What happens?
cards.a:
The popup never appears, because the IDs differ

Popup IDs follow the ID stack, so both calls must be made at the same PushID level.

cards.q: When should you use a modal popup?
cards.a:
For a decision needed before continuing, such as unsaved changes

Modals block everything else until answered. Information belongs in a tooltip or a log.

cards.q: What does SetDragDropPayload do with the data you pass?
cards.a:
It copies the bytes, so pass values such as ids rather than pointers

The copy stays valid even if the source changes. A copied pointer still points at the original object, which is why you pass ids or indexes.

cards.q: When does AcceptDragDropPayload return non-null?
cards.a:
On the frame the mouse button is released over the target with a payload of the accepted type

Without extra flags it only delivers on the drop. `ImGuiDragDropFlags_AcceptBeforeDelivery` lets you peek while hovering.

cards.q: What check must re-parenting by drag and drop make?
cards.a:
That the new parent is not the dragged node itself or any of its descendants

Otherwise the node becomes its own ancestor, a loop that detaches the whole branch from the tree.

cards.q: What is a drag-and-drop payload's type string for?
cards.a:
So a target only accepts payloads it understands

A texture slot accepts "ASSET" and ignores "ENTITY", and only matching targets highlight while dragging.

cards.q: Why apply a list reorder after the loop that draws the list?
cards.a:
Changing the vector while iterating over it skips or repeats items

Record the move during the loop, then apply it once the loop is done.

cards.q: Node A is the parent of B, and B the parent of C. Can A be dropped onto C?
cards.a:
No; A would become a descendant of itself

C is A's descendant, so making C A's parent creates a loop.

cards.q: What two config flags turn on docking and multiple viewports?
cards.a:
`ImGuiConfigFlags_DockingEnable` and `ImGuiConfigFlags_ViewportsEnable`

Both go into `io.ConfigFlags` once after creating the context, on the docking branch. The `ImGuiDockNodeFlags` are for individual dock nodes.

cards.q: What extra calls does the loop need with multiple viewports?
cards.a:
`ImGui::UpdatePlatformWindows` and `ImGui::RenderPlatformWindowsDefault` after rendering the main window

The first creates, moves and resizes the OS windows; the second renders and presents each one.

cards.q: How do you give first-time users a sensible layout?
cards.a:
Build it with the DockBuilder API when the dockspace has no saved layout, and offer it again from a reset menu item

Rebuilding it every frame would wipe whatever the user arranged; after the first run, `imgui.ini` remembers their layout.

cards.q: What is a dock node?
cards.a:
Either a leaf holding windows as tabs, or a split holding two child nodes with a ratio

A dockspace is a tree of dock nodes, and the splits divide the space.

cards.q: A split node 1000 pixels wide is split left/right with ratio 0.2. How wide is the left child?
cards.a:
200 pixels

The first child gets ratio times the size along the split axis: 0.2 x 1000 = 200. The second child gets the remaining 800.

cards.q: What does `ImGuiDockNodeFlags_PassthruCentralNode` do?
cards.a:
Keeps the empty centre see-through so the scene shows and gets clicks

Editors draw their 3D view behind ImGui, visible through that empty central area.

cards.q: How do you change a style value for just one widget?
cards.a:
`PushStyleColor` or `PushStyleVar` before it and the matching Pop after it

The Push/Pop pair limits the change to what is drawn in between; changing the style object directly changes it for everything until you change it back.

cards.q: How should a tool handle a 200% display scale?
cards.a:
Multiply the style sizes with `ScaleAllSizes` and load fonts at the scaled pixel size

`ScaleAllSizes` covers paddings, spacing and roundings but not fonts, and a small font scaled up looks blurry, so load fonts at the real size.

cards.q: Why are ImGui labels UTF-8, and what does that mean for icons?
cards.a:
ImGui reads strings as UTF-8, so icons are written as their UTF-8 byte sequences

Icon code points sit in the private use area: U+F0C7, for example, is written as the three bytes `EF 83 87`. A header of named constants usually does this for you.

cards.q: What does `style.ScaleAllSizes(2.0f)` change?
cards.a:
Paddings, spacings, roundings and other sizes, but not the font

Load the font at the scaled size separately.

cards.q: Why merge an icon font into the text font?
cards.a:
So one string can mix words and icons without switching fonts

`MergeMode` adds the icon glyphs to the previously added font, so "\xef\x83\x87 Save" draws an icon and a word.

cards.q: How many bytes does the code point U+F0C7 take in UTF-8?
cards.a:
Three

Code points from U+0800 to U+FFFF use three bytes; four bytes start at U+10000.

cards.q: Describe the format of imgui.ini.
cards.a:
`[Type][Name]` section headers, each followed by `Key=Value` lines

Sections cover windows, tables, docking and any custom handlers. It is a simple text format, which is why a custom settings handler can add its own sections.

cards.q: What must be true of the string assigned to `io.IniFilename`?
cards.a:
It must stay valid for as long as ImGui uses it, because ImGui stores only the pointer

A temporary `std::string`'s `c_str()` dies at the end of the statement and ImGui would read freed memory, so keep the string static or global.

cards.q: When must custom settings handlers be added?
cards.a:
Before the first `NewFrame`, because that is when the ini file is read

Added later, the ini file has already been read and your section is ignored.

cards.q: Why should imgui.ini not stay in the working directory?
cards.a:
The working directory depends on how the program is started, so settings appear lost

Started from Visual Studio, a shortcut or a terminal, the program can get different working directories. Use a fixed per-user settings folder.

cards.q: What does a settings handler let you do?
cards.a:
Store your tool's own settings as sections of the same ini file

Your data then loads and saves together with the window layout.

cards.q: How do you implement named layouts?
cards.a:
Keep strings from `SaveIniSettingsToMemory` and apply one with `LoadIniSettingsFromMemory`

A layout is just the ini text, so a map from name to string holds them all.

cards.q: How does a ring buffer feed a scrolling graph?
cards.a:
New samples overwrite the oldest; the offset says where the oldest sample is

Nothing moves in the fixed array: the write position goes round it, and `values_offset` tells PlotLines to start drawing at the oldest sample.

cards.q: Name two ways to smooth a noisy value.
cards.a:
A moving average over the last N samples, and exponential smoothing: `smoothed += (value - smoothed) * k`

The moving average uses the samples already in the ring buffer; exponential smoothing needs no buffer at all.

cards.q: How do you map a value to a y position in a custom graph?
cards.a:
`y = top + height * (1 - (value - min) / (max - min))`

Screen y grows downwards, so the fraction is flipped with `1 -`: larger values get smaller y and appear higher.

cards.q: What is the `values_offset` argument of PlotLines for?
cards.a:
It says where the oldest sample of a ring buffer is, so the graph scrolls without moving data

Pass the ring buffer's write position once it is full.

cards.q: A ring buffer of 120 samples is full and its next write position is 37. Where is the oldest sample?
cards.a:
At index 37

The next write overwrites the oldest sample, so the oldest is where the next write will go. Index 36 is the newest.

cards.q: When should you use ImPlot instead of PlotLines?
cards.a:
When you need axes, zooming, legends or several series

PlotLines is a quick single-series graph; ImPlot is a companion library with its own context for full charts.

cards.q: Describe ImGuiTextFilter's syntax.
cards.a:
Comma-separated terms, ignoring case; a `-` term excludes, others include

Terms are checked in order and the first one found in the line decides; if none is found, the line passes only when there are no inclusions.

cards.q: How do you make logging thread-safe?
cards.a:
Protect the entries with a mutex, or have threads push into a queue the UI thread drains each frame

Two threads pushing into a vector at once corrupt it; `static` changes its lifetime, not its safety.

cards.q: How do you keep filtering cheap?
cards.a:
Recompute the list of matching indexes only when the filter changes, and check only new entries as they arrive

Then the per-frame cost depends on the new lines and the clipper's visible rows, not the size of the log.

cards.q: Which lines does the filter `-missing,texture` show?
cards.a:
Lines containing "texture" but not "missing"

Terms are checked in order: the exclusion comes first and hides "missing" lines, then the inclusion shows "texture" lines.

cards.q: With the filter `texture,-missing`, is the line "texture missing" shown?
cards.a:
Yes: "texture" matches first and decides

The first matching term decides, so put exclusions first.

cards.q: A filter contains only `-vsync`. What passes?
cards.a:
Every line that does not contain "vsync"

With no inclusions, every line that is not excluded passes.

cards.q: How does a log window stay fast with a million entries?
cards.a:
Keep an index of matching entries, update it as lines arrive, draw it with the clipper

The clipper submits only the visible rows, and the index list avoids refiltering everything.

cards.q: How does a field table let one function inspect any type?
cards.a:
Each entry gives a field's name, kind and offset, so the function can find the field inside any object and pick the right widget

The offset locates the field inside whatever object is passed, and the kind chooses Checkbox, DragFloat, ColorEdit3 and so on.

cards.q: How should an inspector show a field for several selected objects?
cards.a:
Normally if all values are equal, as mixed if they differ, and an edit writes the new value to every selected object

Users expect an edit to apply to everything selected, and a made-up average would hide that the values differ.

cards.q: What must be true of a type for `offsetof` to be reliable?
cards.a:
It must be standard-layout, such as a plain struct with no virtual functions

`offsetof` is only guaranteed for standard-layout types (no virtual functions, no mixed access specifiers), so keep inspectable component data in plain structs.

cards.q: Why describe a type's fields in a table?
cards.a:
One table drives the inspector, saving, loading, copy and paste and undo for every type

It is a small reflection system that you write once; ImGui itself knows nothing about it.

cards.q: Three selected lights have intensities 5, 5 and 8. What should the intensity field show?
cards.a:
A mixed value, such as "--"

Values that differ are shown as mixed until the user edits them.

cards.q: What does `offsetof(Light, intensity)` give?
cards.a:
The byte position of `intensity` inside a `Light`

Add it to an object's address (as a `char*`) to reach the field.

cards.q: Describe the do, undo and redo operations on two stacks.
cards.a:
Do: apply, push on undo, clear redo. Undo: pop undo, revert, push on redo. Redo: pop redo, apply, push on undo

Each change moves between the two stacks, and a new change clears redo because that history no longer exists.

cards.q: Why should changes store ids rather than pointers?
cards.a:
Objects can be deleted and recreated by undo at a different address; ids stay valid

Undoing a delete makes a new object, so a pointer to the old one would dangle.

cards.q: How does a group of changes undo correctly?
cards.a:
It reverts its changes in the reverse order they were applied

Later changes may depend on earlier ones, so they must be undone first.

cards.q: The user undoes twice, then makes a new change. What happens to the redo stack?
cards.a:
It is cleared

Those undone changes belong to a history that no longer exists; redoing them on top of the new state could make no sense.

cards.q: How do you record one undo step for a whole slider drag?
cards.a:
Save the value on `IsItemActivated`; record on `IsItemDeactivatedAfterEdit`

That gives one step from the value before the drag to the value after it. Record it without applying it again, since the value is already set.

cards.q: Why does a saved marker work better than a dirty flag?
cards.a:
Undoing back to the saved state makes the document clean again

Compare the current undo position with the position at the last save; a plain flag cannot tell that you got back there.

cards.q: Why does zooming need to adjust the pan?
cards.a:
To keep the point under the mouse in place; otherwise the view jumps towards the origin with every zoom step

Remember which tile is under the mouse before zooming, then move the pan so it is under the cursor again.

cards.q: Why use an InvisibleButton over the canvas?
cards.a:
It gives hover, active and click state, and stops drags from moving the window

The draw list only draws; the invisible button is the item covering the whole canvas that ImGui's item queries and clicks refer to.

cards.q: Why should flood fill not be recursive?
cards.a:
A large region needs one call per tile, which can overflow the call stack; an explicit stack or queue cannot

The explicit stack or queue lives on the heap and grows as needed, so even a huge region is fine.

cards.q: How many undo steps should one paint stroke (press, drag across 30 tiles, release) record?
cards.a:
One, holding every changed tile's old value, recorded on release

Collect the changed tiles while the button is held and record them as a single step, as in lesson 5.04's "one drag, one step".

cards.q: How do begin and end events become a tree?
cards.a:
Walk them in order with a stack: a begin pushes a child of the current top; an end pops the top and records its duration

The stack's top is always the zone that is currently open, so every begin knows its parent.

cards.q: What is the difference between total and self time?
cards.a:
Total time is the whole span of a zone; self time is the total minus the time spent in its child zones

Self time is the time spent in that zone's own code, not in the zones nested inside it.

cards.q: Why should zone names be string literals?
cards.a:
Their pointers stay valid forever, so recording a zone costs no allocation or copying

A literal lives for the whole program, so storing just the `const char*` is safe and cheap.

cards.q: A zone "update" lasts 51 ms and has child zones of 28 ms and 19 ms. What is its self time?
cards.a:
4 ms

Self time is total minus the children's totals: 51 - (28 + 19) = 4 ms. 47 ms is the children's sum, not the remainder.

cards.q: Name the three choices for ImGui in a shipped game.
cards.a:
Compile it out, keep it hidden behind a key or flag, or keep some tools as real player-facing features

Most shipped games compile it out; hidden tools suit test builds, and shipped tools must be treated as real product UI.
cards.lessonTitle: ImGui in a Game You Ship

cards.q: Where does ImGui's cost usually come from?
cards.a:
CPU time building debug windows each frame, mostly ones that loop over many objects

The GPU work is usually a few draw calls, and most memory goes to the font atlas. Use the clipper and only build windows that are open.
cards.lessonTitle: ImGui in a Game You Ship

cards.q: What must you check about input when tools are hidden?
cards.a:
That nothing can take keyboard or mouse focus while hidden, so the game always receives its input

If a hidden window kept focus, the game would stop reacting to keys while showing no reason why.
cards.lessonTitle: ImGui in a Game You Ship

cards.q: What should happen to cheat-like debug tools in an online game's client?
cards.a:
Compile them out, and make sure the server does not trust the client anyway

Hidden tools can still be found and enabled; compiled-out code cannot. Even then, the server decides what is allowed.
cards.lessonTitle: ImGui in a Game You Ship

cards.q: What does the MIT licence require when you ship Dear ImGui?
cards.a:
Including the licence text with the software

It is a permissive licence: free for commercial use as long as the licence text is included, usually in an "open source licences" screen or file.
cards.lessonTitle: ImGui in a Game You Ship

cards.q: Why put debug UI code in its own files?
cards.a:
So the shipping build can leave whole files out

A build switch is cleaner at the file level, and without the tools the shipping build may not need to link ImGui at all.
cards.lessonTitle: ImGui in a Game You Ship
